section.title: The Extreme Value Theorem: Proof Outline
section.p: The Extreme Value Theorem says that a continuous function on a closed and bounded interval reaches its highest and lowest values.
The theorem sounds visually obvious. But each word is doing work.
This section explains why completeness is hiding behind that statement.

subsection.title: Why the function is bounded
subsection.p: First we explain why a continuous function on [a,b] cannot blow up.
Suppose, for contradiction, that f is not bounded above on [a,b].
Bisect the interval [a,b]. If f were bounded above on both halves, then it would be bounded above on the whole interval. So at least one half must still have no upper bound.
Choose such a half. Bisect it again. Again choose a half where f is not bounded above.

subsection.title: Why the hypotheses matter
subsection.p: The hypotheses of the Extreme Value Theorem cannot be removed.

paragraphs.title: Missing endpoint
paragraphs.p: is continuous on its domain, but it has no absolute maximum and no absolute minimum.
The values approach 1, but never reach 1. They approach 0, but never reach 0.
The problem is that the interval is not closed.

paragraphs.title: Unbounded interval
paragraphs.p: is continuous and the interval is closed, but the interval is not bounded. The function has a minimum value 0, but no maximum.

paragraphs.title: Discontinuity
paragraphs.p: The function is defined on the closed bounded interval [0,1], but it is not continuous at 1. Its values get arbitrarily close to 1, but no input gives value 1.
So g has no absolute maximum.

note.title: Closed, bounded, continuous
note.p: Each word in the Extreme Value Theorem protects against a different failure.
